catalog_quote: In this study, the term 'tone' is used to classify the pitch on individual syllables. The pitches are arranged in certain patterns termed 'tone patterns'. The term 'intonation' is used for modifications of an entire tone pattern, e.g., raising the general pitch level while the relation of the individual tones to each other remains constant. ... There are three phonetic ranges of pitch, and there are restrictions on the distribution of the top and middle ranges. ... The system is analysed as having two contrasting tonemes, low tone and high tone, plus a feature of upstep which gives rise to the top pitch. The upstep feature is of two types: automatic upstep and the upstep toneme which are described below. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every segment of the deciding quotation and the domain quotation is verbatim in the held Rosetta excerpt at the stated sections/pages (2.3/2.3.1 pp. 11-12; 2.5 p. 17). (2) Deciding source: Thomas 1978 is the standard and only reference grammar of Engenni (published SOAS 1969 thesis); Glottolog lists no later grammar, phonology monograph or instrumental study, and the later tone literature (Thomas 1974, Snider 1999 JWAL, Hyman 2000) is built entirely on Thomas's data and uniformly treats Engenni as a two-tone (H/L) language with upstep/three surface levels; none mentions stress or accent. (3) I fetched sources the full 201-page book (previously we held only ch. 2) and scanned it: 'stress'/'accent' occur nowhere, so the 'no word stress described' claim now holds for the whole grammar, not just the phonology chapter; Snider 1999 (open, fetched sources) confirms the tonal analysis. Remaining

sources.citation: Snider, Keith L. 1999 [1998/99]. Tonal 'upstep' in Engenni. Journal of West African Languages 27(1): 3-15.
sources.quote: p. 3: 'Engenni, a Kwa language spoken in Nigeria, has three levels of surface pitch with restrictions on the top and middle levels. There are only two contrasting tones: low and high. In addition there is what Thomas (1978) calls "automatic upstep."' Reanalyses upstep as non-downstepped H within Register Tier Theory; fn. 2: 'All data in this article are taken from Thomas (1974, 1978).' No mention of stress or accent.
sources.locator: abstract p. 3; sec. 1 p. 3 and fn. 2
